subject: AI & Agents
title: Deep Blue Defeats Kasparov
description: A micro-lesson that makes Deep Blue Defeats Kasparov usable.

hook.text: May 11, 1997. The world chess champion stares at the board, stunned. A machine just beat him.

buildup.text: IBM's Deep Blue evaluated 200 million positions per second using brute-force search.

discovery.text: It combined raw computation with hand-tuned chess knowledge from grandmasters.

twist.text: Kasparov accused IBM of cheating. IBM refused a rematch and dismantled Deep Blue.

climax.text: The world realized machines could conquer games once thought to require human genius.

punchline.text: The king fell to a calculator with great taste in moves.

quiz.question: How did Deep Blue play chess?
options: Brute-force search evaluating millions of positions per second
Neural networks trained on chess games

details.summary: In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match. It was the first time a computer beat a reigning world champion under standard tournament conditions.
details.whyItMatters: Deep Blue proved machines could outperform the best human minds at complex intellectual tasks. The event captured global attention and shifted public perception of AI capabilities.
takeaways: Deep Blue defeated Kasparov in a six-game match in 1997
It used brute-force search evaluating 200 million positions per second
The match was a cultural turning point for AI public perception

faq.question: How did Deep Blue play chess?
faq.answer: Deep Blue used specialized hardware to evaluate 200 million chess positions per second using brute-force search. It combined this with evaluation functions tuned by grandmasters, rather than learning from games.

faq.question: Did Deep Blue prove that AI is smarter than humans?
faq.answer: No. Deep Blue was narrowly specialized for chess and could not do anything else. It demonstrated that computers could outperform humans at one specific complex task, not that they possessed general intelligence.
